CT unenhanced attenuation under 10 Hounsfield units (HU) indicates high intracytoplasmic lipid content pathognomonic of benign adrenal adenoma; absolute contrast washout >60% confirms benignity.
Pheochromocytoma arises from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, diagnosed by 3- to 4-fold elevations of plasma or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and normetanephrines.

Preoperative alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine (10 mg twice daily titrated for 10 to 14 days) is mandatory in pheochromocytoma prior to starting beta-blockade, preventing catastrophic hypertensive crisis from unopposed alpha-agonism.

Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) features hypertension and hypokalemia; screened via plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR >20 to 30) and confirmed with adrenal vein sampling (AVS) for lateralization.
Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) is characterized by size >4 cm to 6 cm, unenhanced CT attenuation >20 HU, delayed washout <40%, and heterogeneous necrosis/calcification.
Laparoscopic transperitoneal or retroperitoneal adrenalectomy is the gold standard approach for benign functioning lesions and solitary adrenal metastases measuring under 6 cm.

Adrenal biopsy (percutaneous fine-needle core biopsy) is strictly contraindicated in pheochromocytoma and primary resectable ACC, reserved solely for confirming metastatic disease from a known extra-adrenal primary.

modules.name: Renal Transplantation: Surgical Techniques and Complications

topics.title: Renal Transplantation: Donor Nephrectomy, Allograft Implantation and Urological Complications
topics.book: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology 12e Ch 88 (Urologic Complications of Renal Transplantation)

mustKnow.fact: Laparoscopic donor nephrectomy preferentially harvests the left kidney due to its significantly longer renal vein compared to the short right renal vein which drains directly into the IVC.
Heterotopic allograft placement implants the donor kidney into the recipient iliac fossa extraperitoneally, with allograft renal artery anastomosed to external iliac or internal iliac artery.
Extravesical Lich-Gregoir ureteroneocystostomy with a double-J stent is the standard technique for allograft ureteral implantation, carrying the lowest rates of urological leak and obstruction.
Ureteral stenosis (2% to 5%) in the transplant allograft typically arises from distal ureteral ischemia secondary to devascularization of the donor lower pole ureteral blood supply during harvest.

Urine leak after renal transplantation (1% to 4%) presents with rising serum creatinine, pelvic pain, and wound drainage; fluid analysis shows creatinine concentration significantly higher than serum creatinine.

Lymphocele (1% to 15%) results from unligated recipient iliac lymphatics; symptomatic fluid collections compressing the allograft vein or ureter are treated via laparoscopic peritoneal fenestration (marsupialization).
Renal artery stenosis in the allograft presents with refractory hypertension and unexplained graft dysfunction, managed primarily with percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) and stenting.
Transplant renal vein thrombosis is a catastrophic complication causing sudden oliguria, severe allograft swelling, and graft loss, occurring in <1% to 2% within the first 48 to 72 hours.

modules.name: Renal Renovascular Disease and Renal Artery Aneurysms

topics.title: Renovascular Hypertension: Atherosclerotic vs Fibromuscular Dysplasia and Renal Aneurysms
topics.book: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology 12e Ch 86 (Renal Physiology and Renovascular Hypertension)

mustKnow.fact: Renal artery stenosis causes renovascular hypertension via activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (Goldblatt two-kidney, one-clip model).
Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis (90% of cases) involves the ostium and proximal third of the main renal artery in older patients with generalized vascular disease.

Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD, 10% of cases) typically affects young females, involving the middle and distal segments and branches, displaying a pathognomonic string-of-beads appearance on angiography.
Medial fibroplasia is the most common subtype of FMD (85%), characterized by alternating zones of collagenous fibromuscular hyperplasia and thinned media.
Percutaneous transluminal renal angioplasty (PTRA) without stenting achieves high cure rates (>80%) for FMD, whereas atherosclerotic disease mandates stent placement.

Renal artery aneurysms (RAA) are saccular or fusiform dilatations, with surgical or endovascular repair indicated when size exceeds 2 cm, or in women of childbearing age due to pregnancy rupture risk.
Renal arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) are congenital cirsoid communications between renal arteries and veins, presenting with massive gross hematuria and managed with transcatheter embolization.
Acquired renal arteriovenous fistulae (AVFs) commonly follow percutaneous renal biopsy or trauma, presenting with audible flank bruit, hypertension, and high-output cardiac failure.

modules.name: Urological Instrumentation, Lasers and Laparoscopic Physics

topics.title: Urological Physics: Optics, Electrosurgery Modalities, Laser Physics and Laparoscopic Access
topics.book: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology 12e Ch 13-15 (Endoscopy, Laparoscopy, and Energy Modalities)

mustKnow.fact: Rigid optical telescopes employ the Hopkins rod-lens optical system, which replaces traditional glass lenses with long glass rods separated by thin air spaces, increasing light transmission and resolution.

Endoscope viewing angles include 0-degree (straight ahead, ureterorenoscopy/diagnostic cystoscopy), 30-degree (standard inspection), 70-degree (lateral wall and dome), and 120-degree (retrograde bladder neck inspection).
Monopolar electrosurgery completes the circuit through a patient return electrode pad; stray current can cause unrecognized visceral injury via direct coupling or insulation failure.

Bipolar electrosurgery confines electrical current between active and return electrodes located on the instrument tip, eliminating patient ground pads and functioning safely in conductive saline solutions.

Pneumoperitoneum for laparoscopic urology is established with carbon dioxide (CO2) due to high solubility in blood, non-flammability, and rapid pulmonary clearance, maintaining intra-abdominal pressure at 12 to 15 mmHg.
Hypercarbia and respiratory acidosis during prolonged laparoscopy result from peritoneal CO2 absorption, managed by ventilatory adjustment (increasing minute ventilation) by the anesthesiologist.
Hasson open technique achieves access under direct visual control without blind needle puncture, recommended in patients with prior abdominal surgery to prevent mesenteric/bowel laceration.
Ultrasonic shears (Harmonic scalpel) vibrate longitudinally at 55.5 kHz to denature proteins and seal vessels up to 5 mm in diameter with minimal lateral thermal spread (under 1 mm).
